## Today's Lecture
:::
In today's lecture we will cover:

-   Why bagging is not enough
-   The idea behind random forests
-   The random forest algorithm
-   Out of bag error and variable importance
-   Tuning a random forest
-   Random forests in R
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Why Random Forests?
:::

Random forests are among the most successful and widely used machine learning
models. Many people treat them as the default first model for prediction from
tables of data, because they:

-   need little tuning,
-   handle nonlinear effects and interactions on their own,
-   work with both categorical and continuous predictors, and
-   hold up well against noise and overfitting.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Where We Left Off
:::

Random forests build directly on the last two lectures, so we start with a
quick recap: a single decision tree, then bagging.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
-   Why does a single tree overfit?
-   Why does averaging many trees help?
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Recap: A Single Decision Tree
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| cache: true
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| out-width: "55%"
#| fig-align: center
# the same tree as the decision tree lecture: same data, split, seed, and settings
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(rpart); library(rattle); library(caret); library(rsample); library(recipes)
})

recap_data <- read.csv("data/data-final-shuffled.csv")
recap_cats <- c(colnames(recap_data)[sapply(recap_data, class) == "character"],
                colnames(recap_data)[sapply(recap_data, max) == 1])
recap_data[recap_cats] <- lapply(recap_data[recap_cats], as.factor)

set.seed(123)
recap_split <- initial_split(recap_data, prop = 0.7, strata = "OPN8")

set.seed(15)
recap_tree <- train(
  recipe(OPN8 ~ ., data = training(recap_split)) %>%
    step_impute_bag(all_predictors()) %>%
    step_dummy(all_factor_predictors(), one_hot = FALSE),
  data       = training(recap_split),
  method     = "rpart",
  metric     = "Kappa",
  trControl  = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
  tuneLength = 10
)

fancyRpartPlot(recap_tree$finalModel, sub = "")
```

-   A tree grows by greedy splits: at each node, it takes the split that most
    reduces impurity.
-   `cp` limits its size, and cross validation chooses `cp`. Our tree had 4
    leaves, split first on `OPN1`, and reached a test Kappa of 0.469.
-   Its weakness is instability. Depending only on how the folds were drawn,
    cross validation chose trees with anywhere from 2 to 17 leaves.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Recap: Bagging
:::

Bagging, short for bootstrap aggregating, fixes that instability by averaging:

1.  Draw many bootstrap samples: each the same size as the data, sampled with
    replacement.
2.  Grow a deep, unpruned tree on each sample. Each tree has low bias and high
    variance.
3.  Combine the trees: majority vote for classification, average for
    regression.

Each tree overfits its own sample in its own way. Averaging many of them cancels
out much of that variance.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### How the Trees Combine
:::

Here is one new respondent passed through 5 bagged trees. Each tree classifies
the respondent on its own, and then we count the votes.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3
library(ggplot2)

# five small trees; the highlighted path is where the new respondent goes
centers <- c(1, 3.5, 6, 8.5, 11)
left_var  <- c("EXT9", "OPN5", "CSN5", "OPN10", "EXT2")
right_var <- c("OPN1", "EXT9", "OPN10", "AGR4", "OPN2")
leaf_class <- list(c(0, 0, 0, 1), c(0, 1, 1, 0), c(0, 0, 0, 1),
                   c(0, 0, 0, 1), c(1, 0, 1, 0))
leaf_hit <- c(4, 3, 3, 4, 3)  # every tree sends the respondent right at OPN1

nodes <- edges <- leaves <- NULL
for (b in 1:5) {
  x  <- centers[b]
  lx <- x + c(-0.9, -0.3, 0.3, 0.9)
  on_right <- leaf_hit[b] > 2
  nodes <- rbind(nodes, data.frame(
    x = c(x, x - 0.6, x + 0.6), y = c(4, 3, 3),
    label = c("OPN1", left_var[b], right_var[b]),
    on_path = c(TRUE, !on_right, on_right)))
  edges <- rbind(edges, data.frame(
    x = c(x, x, x - 0.6, x - 0.6, x + 0.6, x + 0.6),
    y = c(4, 4, 3, 3, 3, 3),
    xend = c(x - 0.6, x + 0.6, lx), yend = c(3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 2),
    on_path = c(!on_right, on_right, 1:4 == leaf_hit[b])))
  leaves <- rbind(leaves, data.frame(
    x = lx, y = 2, class = factor(leaf_class[[b]], levels = c(0, 1)),
    hit = 1:4 == leaf_hit[b]))
}
# leaves the respondent did not reach are drawn in pale colors
leaves$fill <- ifelse(leaves$hit,
                      c("#41ab5d", "#3182bd")[leaves$class],
                      c("#d4ecd0", "#d3e3f3")[leaves$class])
votes <- leaves[leaves$hit, ]

ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend,
                                 color = on_path, linewidth = on_path)) +
  geom_segment(data = votes, aes(x, y - 0.25, xend = 6, yend = 0.7),
               color = "grey55", arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.1, "in"))) +
  geom_label(data = nodes, aes(x, y, label = label,
                               fontface = ifelse(on_path, "bold", "plain")),
             size = 4.2, fill = "white", label.size = 0.3) +
  geom_point(data = leaves, aes(x, y, fill = fill), shape = 21, size = 10,
             stroke = 0.6, color = ifelse(leaves$hit, "black", "grey60")) +
  geom_text(data = leaves, aes(x, y, label = class), fontface = "bold",
            size = 5, color = ifelse(leaves$hit, "white", "grey50")) +
  annotate("text", x = centers, y = 4.5, label = paste("Tree", 1:5),
           size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("point", x = 6, y = 0.2, shape = 21, size = 18,
           fill = "#3182bd") +
  annotate("text", x = 6, y = 0.2, label = "1", color = "white",
           fontface = "bold", size = 7) +
  annotate("text", x = 6.8, y = 0.2, hjust = 0, size = 5.5,
           label = "Majority vote: 4 of 5 trees say 1") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("TRUE" = "black", "FALSE" = "grey80")) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c("TRUE" = 1.3, "FALSE" = 0.6)) +
  scale_fill_identity() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 12), ylim = c(-0.1, 4.6), clip = "off") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

-   Each tree sends the respondent down to one leaf. The most common class in
    that leaf is the tree's vote.
-   The class with the most votes wins. Here 4 of the 5 trees vote 1, so we
    predict `OPN8 = 1`.
-   The share of votes, 4 out of 5 or 0.80, serves as the predicted probability.
-   For regression, we average the trees' predicted numbers instead. Random
    forests combine their trees the same way.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Recap: Bagging on the Personality Data
:::

| Test set    | Single tree | 100 bagged trees |
|-------------|------------:|-----------------:|
| Accuracy    | 0.741 | 0.774 |
| Kappa       | 0.469 | 0.543 |
| Sensitivity | 0.654 | 0.752 |
| Specificity | 0.810 | 0.792 |

-   Each bagged tree had more than 80 leaves. Any one of them overfits, but the
    average of 100 predicted better than the single pruned tree.
-   The out of bag error was 0.28, so about 72% of observations were classified
    correctly by the trees that never saw them.
-   The cost: there is no longer a single tree to read.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Bagging Looks Like Cross Validation
:::

Both methods fit many models, each on part of the data, and keep the rest for
checking. Here are 20 observations, split up for 5 models each way.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 4.6
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(559)
n_obs <- 20
n_mod <- 5

# 5 fold cross validation: each observation is held out exactly once
fold <- sample(rep(1:n_mod, each = n_obs / n_mod))
cv_df <- expand.grid(obs = 1:n_obs, model = 1:n_mod)
cv_df$times  <- ifelse(fold[cv_df$obs] == cv_df$model, 0, 1)
cv_df$method <- "5 fold cross validation"

# bagging: each model gets a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement
bag_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:n_mod, function(b) {
  draws <- tabulate(sample(n_obs, replace = TRUE), nbins = n_obs)
  data.frame(obs = 1:n_obs, model = b, times = draws)
}))
bag_df$method <- "Bagging: 5 bootstrap samples"

viz <- rbind(cv_df, bag_df)
viz$status <- factor(ifelse(viz$times == 0, "Held out (out of bag)",
                     ifelse(viz$times == 1, "Used once", "Used 2 or more times")),
                     levels = c("Used once", "Used 2 or more times", "Held out (out of bag)"))
viz$method <- factor(viz$method, levels = c("5 fold cross validation",
                                            "Bagging: 5 bootstrap samples"))

ggplot(viz, aes(obs, factor(model, levels = n_mod:1), fill = status)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_text(data = subset(viz, times > 1), aes(label = times),
            color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 4) +
  facet_wrap(~ method, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Used once" = "#9ecae1",
                               "Used 2 or more times" = "#2171b5",
                               "Held out (out of bag)" = "#fd8d3c")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 5, 10, 15, 20), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Observation", y = "Model", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid = element_blank())
```

-   In cross validation, every column has **exactly one** orange cell.
-   In bagging, the orange cells fall at random, about 37% of each row, and some
    observations are drawn two or three times (the numbers).
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Same Idea, Different Goal
:::

|   | $k$ fold cross validation | Bagging |
|---|---|---|
| Each model is fit on | $k - 1$ of the $k$ folds | a bootstrap sample, with repeats |
| Held out from each model | one fold, $1/k$ of the data | the out of bag observations, about 37% |
| Each observation is held out | exactly once | by about 37% of the models |
| The models are then | used to estimate error, then set aside | averaged into the final prediction |
| The held out data give us | the cross validation error | the out of bag error |

The key difference: cross validation fits models **to measure** a method, and
bagging fits models **to become** the method. The out of bag error is a cross
validation estimate that bagging gives us for free.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
If the out of bag error comes for free, why do we still use cross validation?
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### One Problem Remains
:::

All 100 bagged trees split first on `OPN1`.

-   In bagging, every tree can choose from every predictor at every split.
-   A strong predictor like `OPN1` wins the first split in nearly every
    bootstrap sample, so the trees end up looking alike.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
If every tree starts with the same question, how different can their
predictions be?
:::
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Why Are Similar Trees a Problem?
:::

When the trees look alike, they make similar predictions, and similar mistakes.
How much averaging helps depends on two things:

$$
\text{Var}(\bar{f}) \approx \rho \sigma^2 + \frac{(1 - \rho)\sigma^2}{B}
$$

-   $\sigma^2$ is the variance of each tree,
-   $\rho$ is the correlation between the trees' predictions, and
-   $B$ is the number of trees.

Adding trees shrinks only the second term. If $\rho$ is large, the first term
dominates, and more trees barely help. Averaging 100 identical trees gives you
the same tree.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### How Can We Fix This?
:::

Make the trees less alike by adding **randomness** to how each one is grown.

Random forests do this by **choosing a random subset of predictors at each
split**. Then:

-   different trees see different predictors,
-   they grow differently,
-   their errors are less correlated, and
-   averaging them reduces variance much more.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### A Brief History
:::

-   In 1995, Tin Kam Ho at Bell Labs grew trees on random subsets of the
    predictors and combined them, calling the result "random decision forests."
-   In 1997, Yali Amit and Donald Geman used randomly chosen splits to build
    many trees for recognizing handwritten shapes.
-   In 2001, Leo Breiman, who had introduced bagging in 1996, combined bagging
    with random predictor subsets at each split in his paper "Random Forests."
    He also showed how to use the out of bag observations to estimate error and
    variable importance.

Breiman's version is the one in nearly every software package today.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## What Is a Random Forest?
:::

A random forest is an ensemble of decision trees, each trained on:

-   a different bootstrap sample of the data, like bagging, and
-   a random subset of the predictors at each split.

Each tree makes a prediction, and the forest combines them:

-   by majority vote for classification, and
-   by averaging for regression.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### A Random Subset of Predictors
:::

A single tree, and every bagged tree, searches **all** predictors for the best
split. A random forest changes this one step:

-   At each split, draw a random subset of $m$ predictors.
-   Find the best split among those $m$ only.

Typical defaults, where $p$ is the number of predictors:

-   classification: $m = \sqrt{p}$
-   regression: $m = p / 3$

With $m = p$, a random forest is the same as bagging.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Random Predictors at Each Split
:::

Six trees pick their first split from the same 9 predictors, listed from
strongest to weakest. A random forest with $m = 3$ draws 3 of them per split.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.4
library(ggplot2)

# an illustration with p = 9 predictors, listed from strongest to weakest
preds <- c("OPN1", "OPN10", "OPN2", "OPN5", "EXT9", "AGR4", "CSN5", "EXT2",
           "AGR7")

# m = 3 predictors drawn for the first split of each random forest tree
subsets <- list(c("OPN1", "EXT2", "AGR4"), c("OPN5", "EXT9", "AGR7"),
                c("OPN10", "CSN5", "EXT2"), c("OPN2", "OPN1", "AGR7"),
                c("EXT9", "AGR4", "CSN5"), c("OPN2", "OPN5", "EXT2"))

# the strongest predictor that can be used wins the split
splits <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:6, function(b) {
  in_subset <- preds %in% subsets[[b]]
  rbind(
    data.frame(method = "Bagging: all 9 predictors", tree = b, pred = preds,
               available = TRUE, chosen = preds == "OPN1"),
    data.frame(method = "Random forest: 3 random predictors", tree = b,
               pred = preds, available = in_subset,
               chosen = preds == preds[in_subset][1]))
}))
splits$status <- factor(ifelse(splits$chosen, "Wins the split",
                        ifelse(splits$available, "Can be used", "Not drawn")),
                        levels = c("Can be used", "Wins the split", "Not drawn"))

ggplot(splits, aes(factor(pred, levels = preds), factor(tree, levels = 6:1),
                   fill = status)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ method) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Can be used" = "#9ecae1",
                               "Wins the split" = "#2171b5",
                               "Not drawn" = "#eeeeee")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Tree", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
```

-   Bagging: `OPN1` can always be used, so it wins the first split of every tree.
-   Random forest: `OPN1` is drawn for about 1 in 3 splits. The rest of the
    time, the best predictor in the subset wins.
-   A new subset is drawn at every split, so a tree can still use `OPN1` further
    down.
-   The trees end up less alike, so their mistakes overlap less.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### The Random Forest Algorithm
:::

Given training data with $n$ observations and $p$ predictors:

1.  Choose the number of trees, $B$.
2.  For each tree $b = 1, 2, \ldots, B$:
    1.  Draw a bootstrap sample from the training data.
    2.  Grow a tree on that sample. At each node:
        -   randomly select $m$ predictors,
        -   choose the best split among them, and
        -   keep splitting, with no pruning.
3.  Combine the trees: majority vote for classification, average for
    regression.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Out of Bag Error
:::

As in bagging, each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample, about 63% of the
observations. The other 37% are **out of bag** for that tree.

-   For each observation, predict its outcome using only the trees that did not
    see it.
-   The resulting **out of bag error** estimates error on new data, without
    setting aside a separate validation set.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Variable Importance
:::

A forest has no single tree to read, but it can still tell us which predictors
mattered.

-   **Impurity importance:** add up how much each predictor reduced the Gini
    impurity (or the variance, for regression) across every split that used it,
    in every tree.
-   **Permutation importance:** shuffle one predictor's values and measure how
    much the out of bag error rises. A predictor the forest relies on makes the
    error rise a lot.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Limitations
:::

-   Like bagging, a random forest is much harder to interpret than a single tree.
-   It can be slow to train on large datasets with many trees.
-   It extrapolates poorly beyond the range of the training data, like most tree
    based methods.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Random Forests in R
:::

We fit random forests with the `ranger` package, through `caret::train()` with
`method = "ranger"`. Three settings can be tuned:

| Setting | What it controls |
|---|---|
| `mtry` | How many predictors are drawn at each split |
| `splitrule` | How each split is chosen: `"gini"` for classification, `"variance"` for regression |
| `min.node.size` | When a node stops splitting, which controls how deep each tree grows |

The number of trees, `num.trees`, is not tuned. More trees never hurt a forest;
they only take longer.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Tuning `mtry`
:::

A random forest needs two things that pull against each other:

1.  **Strong trees**, each able to predict well.
2.  **Diverse trees**, which make different mistakes so that averaging helps.

`mtry` sets the balance:

-   A **small** `mtry` adds more randomness: more diverse trees, but each one is
    weaker.
-   A **large** `mtry` gives stronger trees that look more alike. At the
    maximum, it is bagging.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Tuning `min.node.size`
:::

`min.node.size` sets when a node stops splitting. With `min.node.size = 5`:

-   A node with 5 or fewer observations is not split. It becomes a leaf.
-   A node with 6 or more can still split, so leaves can end up smaller than 5.
    A node of 7 can split into 6 and 1.
-   In classification, a leaf that stops early can hold both classes, say 3 to
    2. Its vote is the majority class.

**Smaller** values grow deeper trees, and **larger** values grow shallower ones.

The defaults are 1 for classification and 5 for regression. With 1, a tree keeps
splitting until nearly every leaf holds a single class. Forests usually do well
with deep trees, since averaging removes much of their variance.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Load the Required Packages
:::

```{r}
library(caret)    # train(), confusionMatrix(), and varImp()
library(ranger)   # random forests
library(rsample)  # splitting data into training and test sets
library(recipes)  # dummy coding
library(ggplot2)  # plots
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### The Personality Data Again
:::

The same data, split, and target as the decision tree and bagging lectures:
predicting `OPN8`, "I use difficult words," from the other 49 items.

```{r}
data <- read.csv("data/data-final-shuffled.csv")

# items coded 0 and 1, and items stored as text, are categories
dichotomous_vars <- colnames(data)[sapply(data, max) == 1]
character_vars   <- colnames(data)[sapply(data, class) == "character"]
cat_vars         <- c(character_vars, dichotomous_vars)
data[cat_vars]   <- lapply(data[cat_vars], as.factor)

target <- "OPN8"

set.seed(123)
split      <- initial_split(data, prop = 0.7, strata = target)
data_train <- training(split)
data_test  <- testing(split)
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### The Recipe and the Grid
:::

These data have no missing values, so the recipe only dummy codes the factors.
The grid tries five values of `mtry`, from very random to close to bagging.

```{r}
blueprint <- recipe(OPN8 ~ ., data = data_train) %>%
  step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors())

rf_grid <- expand.grid(
  mtry          = c(2, 4, 7, 15, 30),
  splitrule     = "gini",
  min.node.size = c(1, 5)
)
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Fitting the Forest
:::

Each of the 10 combinations is fit in each of the 10 folds, with 500 trees per
forest.

```{r}
#| cache: true
set.seed(559)

rf_model <- train(
  blueprint,
  data       = data_train,
  method     = "ranger",
  metric     = "Kappa",
  trControl  = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10),
  tuneGrid   = rf_grid,
  num.trees  = 500,
  importance = "impurity"
)
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Tuning Results
:::

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
ggplot(rf_model) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

Cross validated Kappa is highest with `mtry` = `r rf_model$bestTune$mtry` and
`min.node.size` = `r rf_model$bestTune$min.node.size`.
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Test Set Performance
:::

```{r}
pred_rf <- predict(rf_model, newdata = data_test)

cm_rf <- confusionMatrix(pred_rf, data_test$OPN8, positive = "1")

cm_rf$table

round(c(cm_rf$overall[c("Accuracy", "Kappa")],
        cm_rf$byClass[c("Sensitivity", "Specificity")]), 3)
```
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### Comparing Our Models
:::

The same 301 test respondents, across three lectures:

| Test set    | Single tree | Bagged trees | Random forest |
|-------------|------------:|-------------:|--------------:|
| Accuracy    | 0.741 | 0.774 | `r sprintf("%.3f", cm_rf$overall["Accuracy"])` |
| Kappa       | 0.469 | 0.543 | `r sprintf("%.3f", cm_rf$overall["Kappa"])` |
| Sensitivity | 0.654 | 0.752 | `r sprintf("%.3f", cm_rf$byClass["Sensitivity"])` |
| Specificity | 0.810 | 0.792 | `r sprintf("%.3f", cm_rf$byClass["Specificity"])` |

`r if (cm_rf$overall["Kappa"] > 0.543) paste0("Making the trees less alike gives a gain over bagging: Kappa rises from 0.543 to ", sprintf("%.3f", cm_rf$overall["Kappa"]), ".") else "Here the forest does not beat bagging. With these data, the bagged trees were already diverse enough."`
::::

:::: {.slide}
::: {style="color: yellow"}
### What Mattered Most
:::

`varImp()` reports impurity importance, scaled so the most important predictor
scores 100.

:::: {.two-col}
::: {}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 4
ggplot(varImp(rf_model), top = 10) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```
:::

::: {}
::: {.compact}
| Predictor  | Statement |
|------------|-----------|
| `OPN1`     | I have a rich vocabulary. |
| `OPN2`     | I have difficulty understanding abstract ideas. |
| `OPN10_X1` | I am full of ideas. |
| `CSN5`     | I get chores done right away. |
| `OPN7`     | I am quick to understand things. |
:::

-   `OPN10_X1` is the dummy column for `OPN10`, coded 0 and 1.
-   Four of the top five are openness items.
-   `OPN1` is closest in meaning to the target, "I use difficult words."

::: {style="color: yellow"}
## Wrapping Up
:::

-   Bagging averages many trees, but trees that look alike limit how much
    averaging can help.
-   Random forests make the trees less alike by drawing a random subset of
    predictors at each split.
-   `mtry` balances strong trees against diverse trees. With `mtry` equal to the
    number of predictors, a random forest is bagging.
-   The out of bag observations give a built in error estimate, and impurity or
    permutation importance shows which predictors mattered.

::: {style="color: lightgreen"}
Bagging and random forests grow their trees independently. Coming next: what if
each new tree learned from the mistakes of the trees before it?
:::
